{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# The server was part of the appliance.

A connected appliance is often two products sold as one: a thing in your house and a service in somebody else’s data center. The box may be solid, paid for, and screwed to the wall; the essential intelligence lives elsewhere (the server is the invisible half of the appliance). When the vendor closes that service, we call it a “shutdown.” For the owner, it can feel more like repossession.

When I evaluate the damage, I start with a simple inventory. Which commands travel through the cloud? Which records are stored there? Your camera may stop recording events, your thermostat may lose schedules and remote control, and your lights may become ordinary switches. Voice commands, phone alerts, household sharing, integrations, and automation can disappear together. You’ve still got the hardware, but they’ve taken away some of the appliance you bought.

What keeps working after the servers go dark? Sometimes almost everything; sometimes only a manual button (assuming the vendor bothered to provide one). A product that can’t authenticate may refuse to start. An app may open but never connect. A sensor may continue sensing while losing the feature that made its measurements useful. The failure travels from a distant data center to your wall, lock, nursery, or kitchen.

That changes the original bargain. The purchase looked like a sale – money once, appliance yours – but the vendor retained a kill switch over the useful functions. Perhaps the packaging mentioned service dependencies in fine print. Even if it did, that doesn’t make the arrangement fair or intelligible. We accepted the ordinary meaning of “buy”: ownership that survives the seller’s loss of interest.

I call this a landlord hidden inside the machine. You pay for the building, maintain it, supply its electricity, and give it space; the vendor keeps the master key (with no duty to remain in business). When the cloud closes, the company doesn’t merely quit providing an optional extra. It can evict you from functions already installed in your machine. That’s the damn trick concealed by the cheerful word “smart.”

Was the server really part of the appliance? If the device depended on it to perform advertised functions, of course it was. The server was simply located elsewhere and financed through a wager that future revenue would cover its bills. When that wager fails, the vendor’s accounting problem becomes your product failure. We shouldn’t confuse physical distance with separateness.

Local operation breaks that chain. Core controls, schedules, automations, and stored data should run inside the home, without permission from a remote account. Remote access can remain available, but it shouldn’t be the only path. Local credentials and documented interfaces would let another app speak to the device. Exportable data would protect you from lock-in (and protect your household records from vanishing). A local fallback won’t preserve every online feature, but your appliance would keep doing its main job on your network.

This isn’t a demand that every household maintain a miniature data center. Local-first design can be boring: a hub, a web page, a standard protocol, or controls on the device. The principle matters more than the implementation – failure elsewhere shouldn’t disable safe operation here. Manufacturers can still sell cloud conveniences, storage, and support. They just can’t turn the end of those services into the end of your property.

When I shop for connected devices, I’d ask what happens if the app, account system, and vendor all disappear. Can the device still perform its central function? Can another controller replace the official one? Those answers should be on the box, with a promised support period and a shutdown plan. We need rules that treat remote dependencies as parts of the product, because that is how owners encounter them. The server was part of the appliance – ownership should survive it.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o12: named sources and opponents’ attributed terms","why":"The request supplies no verified named source, quotation, or vendor-specific shutdown statement to credit and test."}],"refused":""}
